text.p: Japan's heavyweight corporate investors will be back in the hunt for high-yielding overseas assets after their fiscal year-end hiatus, and analysts say the U.S. will remain a powerful magnet.

A rise in key U.S. interest rates this week for the first time in two years will increase the pull on Japan's cash, they say, as prospects for higher rates in Japan -- where interest rates are among the lowest in the world -- -- remain subdued.

"I don't think it (the U.S. rate hike) will have an impact on the Bank of Japan's policy. We don't see a move in rates until the second half of the year," said Julian Fisher, international economist at Daiwa Europe.
Fisher said Japan's economic recovery was not yet strong enough to merit a rise in rates.

The U.S. Federal Reserve on Tuesday increased its target for the federal funds rate, which banks charge each other for overnight loans, by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. Japan key discount rate, meanwhile, is currently at a record low of 0.50 percent and the lowest in the world.

But Japan is not likely to follow suit, and analysts say after Japanese institutions finish their capital repatriations for their fiscal year-end on March 31, their money will flow back into the U.S. in search of higher yields.
"As long as markets retain a bullish interpretation of what the Fed has been doing, then the U.S. will continue to attract Japanese money," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IBJ International.
Japanese investors are likely to quench their thirst for high-yielders in the 1997/98 fiscal year in the U.S. bond and dollar markets, said analysts.
"The high (bond) yields will be attractive to the Japanese and the high interest rates the Fed is giving will support the dollar," said IBJ's Francis.

Japan's benchmark 10-year government bonds, or JGBs, for example, yielded just 3.03 percent on average in 1996 compared to 6.43 percent for 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds, said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
In the last quarter of 1996, Japanese investors pumped some 4.23 trillion yen ($34.2 billion) into foreign bonds, with over half that going into U.S. bonds.
This compares to 364.8 billion yen siphoned into foreign equities during the same period.
Analysts, however, said the depth of Japanese investors' pockets in the new fiscal year will depend on perceptions over the Fed's future monetary policy.
"If the rate hike is seen as the first of a number of increases, then Japanese investors will wait on the sidelines for 7.25 percent on the U.S. long-bond yield," said Daiwa's Fisher.

But he said a 7.0 percent yield is still seen as very attractive for Japanese investors, adding: "There is no reason at all why Japanese investors will not go in at the 7.0-percent level as soon as the new fiscal year begins." On Thursday the yield on the Treasury's benchmark 30-year long bond was hovering just below 7.00 percent at 6.98 percent.
Coleman, however, said uncertainty over further interest rate rises in the U.S. could keep investors cautious, with some choosing to wait for better yields.

"It may be the case that the flows out of Japan into the U.S. market may not be as large as people expect them to be...We are in a pretty uncertain situation as far as the U.S. is concerned," he said.
And a further tightening on the U.S. monetary front could dampen the outlook for U.S. assets, he added.
"If we do see further tightening, it would signal that the economy is growing too strongly and that there are inflationary pressures. That is a negative backdrop for bond markets," Coleman said.
But even this might not put off Japanese investors who, with trillions of yen to invest overseas, could take advantage of any buying opportunity, analysts said.

"For Japanese institutions, the tendency is still for investing in the U.S... If the market does sell off it will be seen as a buying opportunity by the Japanese and Far Eastern investor bases," said Daiwa's Fisher.
